title: Danube Hits Record Lows, Stranding Cruise Ships and Threatening Energy Across Central Europe
excerpt: Europe's second-longest river has dropped to unprecedented levels in Hungary, Serbia, and Romania, forcing cruise cancellations, grounding a Viking ship, and pushing Hungary toward a nuclear plant shutdown.
body:
• Budapest's Danube water level hit a record low of 9 inches on July 30, shattering the 2013 record, with no significant rain forecast in the coming days.
  • A Viking river ship ran aground in Bulgaria on July 28, while multiple cruise lines have cancelled or rerouted sailings on the Danube and Rhine.
  • Hungary's Paks Nuclear Power Plant — which generates nearly half the country's electricity — faces a complete shutdown as early as next week due to insufficient cooling water.
  • Serbia's largest hydropower plant, Djerdap 1, is producing only a third of its average output, while fuel imports via river barges have dropped to 25% of monthly targets.

A River in Crisis

The Danube, Europe's second-longest river and a lifeline for ten countries from Germany to Romania, has dropped to unprecedented levels this summer. In Budapest, Hungary's national water authority measured a water level of just 9 inches on Wednesday — shattering the previous record low of 13 inches set in 2013, according to the Associated Press.

The cause is straightforward: weeks of relentless heat and virtually no rain across Central and Southeastern Europe. Romania's water authorities reported Danube flow rates plummeting to roughly 1,700 cubic meters per second at the border, compared to a typical July benchmark of 4,700 cubic meters per second. In Serbia, the river measured 38 centimeters below navigation level on July 22 — exceptionally low even for the dry season.

And relief remains elusive. No significant rainfall is forecast for the region in the coming days, though Romania's state water-management agency has indicated levels may gradually rise starting next week following upstream precipitation.

Cruise Ships Stranded and Grounded

The crisis has dealt a severe blow to Europe's river cruise industry, which carries roughly 600,000 passengers annually on the Danube alone. On July 28, a Viking river ship — the Viking Ullur — ran aground on a sandbank in northwest Bulgaria. Passengers were transferred to shore to continue their itinerary, and no injuries were reported.

Hungarian sightseeing operator MAHART-PassNave has reported an 18% drop in bookings in July due to cancellations, with tours to cities north of Budapest suspended entirely.

"River cruise vessels are currently still able to enter Hungary, but several ships are stranded or waiting in ports because of the low water levels."

— Laszlo Somodi, CEO, MAHART-PassNave

The disruptions extend well beyond Hungary. Avalon Waterways has cancelled departures on both the Danube and Rhine. Uniworld's S.S. Emilie, launched earlier this year, was unable to dock in Spitz for a scheduled excursion and had to skip its planned final stops of Regensburg and Nuremberg, substituting Linz instead. AmaWaterways, Riviera Travel, and Viking Cruises have all made adjustments.

For passengers, the fallout ranges from altered excursions and missed ports to lengthy bus transfers. One traveler aboard a Travelmarvel cruise reported being told Budapest was unreachable, only to learn that the substitute docking arrangement also fell through. Others described multi-hour bus rides replacing scenic river passages.

An Energy Crisis in the Making

The drought's consequences extend far beyond tourism. Hungary now faces the prospect of shutting down its Paks Nuclear Power Plant — a facility that generates nearly half the country's electricity — because Danube water used for cooling has become insufficient.

"For the first time in 44 years, the entire Paks Nuclear Power Plant will be completely shut down due to the record-low water level of the Danube. An energy crisis situation may arise from Monday."

— Peter Magyar, Prime Minister of Hungary

In Serbia, the damage is already quantifiable. The country's largest hydropower plant, Djerdap 1 — jointly operated with Romania, with 1,140 MW of installed capacity — is producing only about 5,000 MWh per day, a third of its average output. Serbia's Energy Minister Dubravka Djedovic Handanovic said fuel imports via river have plunged to 25% of their July target, as barges and tankers are forced to operate at 30% to 40% cargo capacity. Coal-fired plants at Kostolac have also cut output due to cooling water shortages.

Djerdap 1's CEO, Dusan Zivkovic, warned that forecasts suggest Danube inflows could drop to around 1,500 cubic meters per second by early August — what he described as "the biological minimum."

A Continent-Wide Pattern

The Danube is not suffering alone. The Rhine, Europe's busiest commercial waterway, has also dropped to levels where ships struggle to pass each other. Lake Brenets, a popular tourist destination on the Switzerland-France border, has nearly dried up entirely as the River Doubs that feeds it has receded. In Croatia, the shrinking Danube exposed the wreck of the cargo ship Fulton, which sank carrying coal in 1937. In Bulgaria, receding waters revealed what researchers believe are ancient mammoth remains — a lower jaw, two tusks, and potentially a rib — along the newly exposed riverbed.

Climate scientists say the pattern is no longer anomalous. "The heat dries the soil, empties the rivers and drives up demand for water all at once. That is the fingerprint of a changing climate," said Hannah Cloke, Regius professor of meteorology and climate science at the University of Reading. "Summers like this are becoming part of the ordinary range, and they will keep getting worse as long as we burn fossil fuels."

What Travelers Should Know

For the large number of Indian travelers who book European river cruises during the summer months, the situation demands attention. Cruise lines are actively restructuring itineraries, and passengers with August bookings on the Danube or Rhine should expect possible changes — from alternative docking points and bus transfers to outright cancellations of specific segments.

Travel insurance policies typically do not cover low-water disruptions, a point raised by concerned travelers on cruise forums. Those with upcoming bookings should contact their cruise operator directly for the latest itinerary status and understand what alternative arrangements are being offered. The disruptions are concentrated on sections upstream of Vilshofen and downstream of Straubing, though this summer's extreme conditions have made the entire river unpredictable.
nri_angle: Indian travelers planning European river cruises this summer face widespread itinerary disruptions and cancellations on the Danube and Rhine.
